one_liner: Binary-only fixed-width B+Tree index for .NET; vendor claims 4.4-7x faster bulk inserts than SQLite (paid Pro build).
what_it_does: An embedded single-file (or in-memory) B+Tree key-value index for .NET Standard 2.0. Keys and values are fixed-length byte buffers whose sizes are set when the tree is created. The API is the class mmh.BTree (CreateMemory / CreateOrOpen / Open, Span-based Insert / Find / Erase, Bof / Next / Prev cursors, Commit / Close) plus IDictionary wrappers from BTreeDictionaryFactory for long, int and fixed-width string keys. It is not SQL and not a drop-in for SQLite, and the engine ships only as a compiled NuGet DLL: the GitHub repo holds docs, an on-disk format spec and a demo.
how_it_is_fast: It has no SQL or VM layer: fixed-width key/value slots sit directly in fixed-size pages (pageSize x 512 bytes, up to 64 KB) and are compared as raw bytes. The vendor attributes the headline numbers mainly to a write-back page cache with deferred flush: dirty pages are written at Commit(), at a byte watermark or by a ~1 s auto-commit, and the PDF gives ~3.16M inserts/s with the cache on vs ~418K/s with it off. Other speed paths are an append fast path for monotonically increasing keys (TryAppendFastPath in the DLL), a bottom-up BulkLoad into an empty tree (0.90 leaf fill) and FNV-1a hash sharding across several trees (ShardManager) for parallel batch inserts. It also has no journal (no WAL or rollback journal), so it avoids the double write SQLite pays for crash safety.
when_to_use: A .NET process that needs a local sorted index over fixed-width keys (big-endian Int64 IDs, Unix timestamps, padded product codes) with small fixed-size values, e.g. a POS/kiosk secondary index or a log keyed by sequence number.
Loading tens of millions to billions of fixed-width records in key order when losing uncommitted work on a crash is acceptable. This is the shape of the published SQLite and PostgreSQL runs.
Hot-path point lookups that must not allocate: Find writes into a caller-supplied Span<byte>, so a SQL engine's parsing and row materialisation are avoided.
You are prepared to evaluate and license the commercial Pro Edition. Every published speedup is for that build (page cache plus Bulk Insert), not for the free package.
when_not_to_use: You need source you can audit, patch or vendor. The engine is closed, and the MIT license covers only the free binary and the docs.

You need crash-safe atomic commits. The NuGet README says it is 'not journaling-based' and has no WAL: power loss during a write can lose the latest uncommitted operation, and consistency is promised only after a successful Commit().
Variable-length keys or values, secondary queries, multi-statement transactions, or concurrent readers. Each tree has one Monitor lock that serialises Find, Insert, Erase and Commit.
You expect the free Community build to be fast. The vendor calls it 'not optimized for speed' (page cache disabled, ~418K inserts/s in the PDF), so the 4.4x/7x figures do not apply to it.

Production-critical use generally. It has 9 GitHub stars, zero issues, one Show HN post with no comments and no independent benchmarks. The release DLL even ships its delete/rebalance test suite as a public class (DeleteEdgeCases) with a hard-coded /home/mmh/... log path and 'ROUTING BUG DETECTED' repro strings.

integration.form: NuGet package (binary-only managed DLL btree.dll, ~137 KB; no source)
integration.dependencies: System.Memory >= 4.5.5 (the netstandard2.0 dependency; the README's 'zero dependencies' ignores it); no native libraries
integration.min_toolchain: .NET Standard 2.0 (.NET Core 2.0+ / .NET Framework 4.6.1+ per the PDF); vendor benchmarks used .NET 9.0
integration.platforms: any .NET runtime; pure managed code. Release notes claim Windows, Linux and ARM edge devices.
integration.thread_safety: Each tree has one Monitor lock. Insert, Find and Erase take it via Monitor.TryEnter with a timeout when bLock=true (the default), so calls are safe but fully serialised, readers included, and a lock timeout raises an exception. Parallelism comes only from ShardManager spreading keys over several trees.

gotchas: In the public 1.3.1 DLL the BTree constructor overwrites the enableCache argument with false (visible in the IL), so CreateOrOpen(..., enableCache: true), as used in the GitHub demo and the PDF, is silently ignored. A public SetUseCache(bool) method with no license check exists, but its behaviour in the free build is not documented.

The docs contradict each other and the binary. The GitHub README shows a new BTree(path, keyLength, ...) constructor in namespace BTreePlus that the DLL does not use (it is mmh.BTree with static factories), and it credits the Community Edition with the cache-on 3M-inserts-in-0.95 s result. The NuGet README lists Erase as free, while NOTICE.md and the PDF call it Enterprise-only. The DLL publicly exposes Erase, BulkLoad, FindRangeValues, PageCache and ShardManager anyway.

Plan capacity up front. max_recs sizes the page allocation table (PAT), and the DLL has 'PAT is full (fixed size)' and 'PAT exhausted after second grow' errors. In-memory trees are capped by the MemoryStream size limit. Count is an int that is recomputed across all leaf pages on each call.

Ordering is raw byte order. Integers must be written big-endian and right-aligned, and strings zero-padded, or range order is wrong. The format spec says over-long keys are truncated to keylen, so distinct long keys can collide.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For .NET, ZoneTree (MIT, source on GitHub, a transactional ACID LSM engine that also reports beating SQLite) is the default pick. Choose BTreePlus only if you want a minimal fixed-width B+Tree file with a published on-disk format that third-party readers can parse, and you are willing to license the closed Pro build to get the advertised speed.
verified_claims_summary: According to the vendor's NuGet README (the only evidence), the paid BTreePlus Pro, using 32 KB pages on NVMe under .NET 9.0/Linux, bulk-inserted 4M rows in 1.03 s vs 4.53 s for SQLite (4.4x) and 1B rows in 346 s vs 2410 s (7x), with no CPU, SQLite pragmas, batching method or harness published. A separate i9-13900 + Samsung 990 PRO run loaded 1B 14-byte records in 5m10s vs PostgreSQL's 6m08s (~1.19x throughput), labelled 'WAL enabled for both engines' even though the same README says BTreePlus has no WAL.
status_note: Maintained: NuGet 1.3.1 shipped in December 2025 and the GitHub docs were updated 2026-01-23 by a single vendor (MMH Systems), but usability is mixed: the free MIT package is binary-only with its page cache forced off, and the advertised speed needs a closed commercial license.
